m6-t1.introduction: Start with a decision, then choose the measurement. Keep the goal, diagnostic numbers and review ritual connected.

sections.title: A metric should change a decision
sections.explanation: Before adding a number to a report, explain what you would do differently if it rose or fell.

items.label: Decision
items.detail: Should the campaign continue, change or pause?

items.label: Evidence
items.detail: Choose a number that informs that choice.

items.label: Guardrail
items.detail: Define the acceptable range or review trigger.

items.label: Action
items.detail: Assign a person and a date to the next step.

sections.takeaway: If no decision could change, the metric may be background context rather than a headline KPI.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Connect outcome, channel and diagnosis
sections.explanation: A useful KPI tree links business progress to the levers you can investigate.

items.label: Search branch
items.detail: Relevant queries → visits → qualified enquiries.

items.label: Social branch
items.detail: Relevant reach → useful clicks → qualified enquiries.

items.label: Lifecycle branch
items.detail: Permission-based follow-up → repeat actions.

items.label: Guardrails
items.detail: Media CPA, lead quality and operational capacity.

sections.takeaway: Record each source and definition. Different platforms may count a “conversion” differently.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 2. The KPI tree, revisited and complete

sections.title: A baseline gives a number context
sections.explanation: The same budget can produce different CPA when customer counts change. Compare like-for-like periods and definitions.

items.label: Previous period
items.detail: Synthetic spend ₹3,000 ÷ 3 acquired customers.

items.label: Current period
items.detail: Synthetic spend ₹3,000 ÷ 4 acquired customers.

sections.takeaway: This shows a 25% CPA reduction. It does not establish why the change happened or whether it will persist.
sections.caption: Synthetic worked example, not live campaign data or an industry benchmark.
sections.section: 3. Baselines and benchmarks: numbers need company

sections.title: The weekly insight ritual
sections.explanation: A weekly report becomes useful when it records a diagnosis and a concrete next action.

items.label: What moved?
items.detail: Compare the defined metric with its baseline.

items.label: Why might it move?
items.detail: List a plausible explanation and competing explanations.

items.label: What next?
items.detail: Choose one test or action with an owner.

items.label: What happened?
items.detail: Review the result at the next agreed checkpoint.

sections.takeaway: Keep the difference between an observed change and a causal explanation explicit.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: A report says “reach increased”. What question makes it decision-ready?
checkpoint.answer: Ask whether relevant people progressed toward the business goal, compared with the right baseline, and what action the evidence supports next. Reach alone is not a verdict.

m6-t2.introduction: See analytics as a chain of events with definitions and verification. Distinguish a meaningful business event from an easy-to-count interaction.

sections.title: Events describe actions, not just pages
sections.explanation: An event records something that happened. Its parameters provide context for interpretation.

items.label: User action
items.detail: A person submits an enquiry successfully.

items.label: Event
items.detail: Record the defined successful-enquiry event once.

items.label: Parameters
items.detail: Attach permitted context such as form type or campaign source.

items.label: Report
items.detail: Aggregate the event using a documented definition.

sections.takeaway: Do not send names, phone numbers, email addresses or other prohibited personal identifiers into analytics.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 1. The event model: everything is an event

sections.title: Installation needs an observed test
sections.explanation: A pasted tag is not proof that the intended business action is counted accurately.

items.label: Plan
items.detail: Specify events, parameters, consent and ownership.

items.label: Install
items.detail: Use the approved implementation route.

items.label: Exercise
items.detail: Complete a test action on the actual site.

items.label: Verify
items.detail: Check the event, parameters and duplicate firing in appropriate debug / realtime views.

sections.takeaway: Keep test traffic identifiable where supported and recheck after site changes.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Five questions, five reporting views
sections.explanation: Start with what you want to know instead of browsing every available chart.

items.label: Who arrived?
items.detail: Read aggregate audience and device context responsibly.

items.label: Where from?
items.detail: Inspect acquisition with consistent campaign tagging.

items.label: What did they use?
items.detail: Review relevant pages and engagement events.

items.label: Where did they leave?
items.detail: Look for journey friction with the available data.

items.label: What action followed?
items.detail: Connect meaningful key events to the business record.

sections.takeaway: An analytics report sees only what the implementation and consent conditions allow it to observe.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. The five questions GA4 answers well

sections.title: Key event choice shapes the story
sections.explanation: Counting a click as a lead can inflate success. Choose a reliable proxy for the actual business action.

items.label: Weak proxy
items.detail: A click on “Send” can happen even when the form fails.

items.label: Stronger event
items.detail: A confirmed successful form submission is closer to an enquiry.

items.label: Business reconciliation
items.detail: A CRM or enquiry log confirms quality and real follow-up.

sections.takeaway: Mark meaningful events deliberately and check whether different systems duplicate or omit the same action.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Observed data is not the whole market
sections.explanation: Consent, blocking, configuration and modelling affect the count. Attribution adds another layer of interpretation.

items.label: Missing observation
items.detail: Some activity is not tracked or cannot be linked.

items.label: Modelled estimates
items.detail: Some reports may include estimates under eligible settings.

items.label: Different definitions
items.detail: Users, sessions, events and customers are not interchangeable.

items.label: Honest reporting
items.detail: State source, window, limitations and reconciliation method.

sections.takeaway: Do not “fix” a mismatch by secretly changing definitions until the totals agree.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: A form button fires an event even when validation fails. Is it a reliable lead count?
checkpoint.answer: No. Track a confirmed successful submission and reconcile with the business enquiry record. Test failed, successful and repeated submissions to detect duplicates.

sections.section: 5. Reading honestly: consent, sampling, attribution noise

m6-t3.introduction: Design a dashboard around five questions, not a wall of charts. Show comparisons, source quality and the next decision.

sections.title: Choose a reporting tool for the job
sections.explanation: The best tool is the one that connects the required sources and can be maintained by the team.

items.label: Connected dashboard
items.detail: Useful for repeatable views over supported data connectors.

items.label: Living spreadsheet
items.detail: Useful for small datasets, manual business records and transparent calculations.

items.label: Hybrid
items.detail: Use a dashboard for trends and a sheet for qualified leads or offline outcomes.

sections.takeaway: A free connector today may change. Document the fallback and ownership.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 1. The tool choice: connected dashboards vs living spreadsheets

sections.title: The five-panel decision page
sections.explanation: Each panel answers a different business question and should use clear titles and units.

items.label: Headline KPIs
items.detail: Are we ahead or behind the comparable previous period?

items.label: Trend + target
items.detail: Are we moving toward the planned outcome?

items.label: Channel breakdown
items.detail: Which sources contribute useful outcomes at what cost?

items.label: Funnel
items.detail: Where are people failing to progress?

items.label: Insight notes
items.detail: What will change, who owns it and by when?

sections.takeaway: A dashboard without a next action is a display, not a management process.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Clean joins before clever charts
sections.explanation: Data sources need compatible dates, definitions and identifiers before totals can be combined responsibly.

items.label: Define
items.detail: Agree event, lead, customer, timezone and currency definitions.

items.label: Connect
items.detail: Record the source and extraction window.

items.label: Reconcile
items.detail: Check duplicates, missing rows and spend totals.

items.label: Label
items.detail: Distinguish observed, estimated and simulated values.

sections.takeaway: Adding conversions from different platforms can double-count the same customer.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Make delivery boring, not blind
sections.explanation: Automated delivery should reduce manual work while preserving an owner for quality and exceptions.

items.label: Refresh
items.detail: Update the agreed sources on schedule.

items.label: Validate
items.detail: Check freshness, missing fields and unexpected totals.

items.label: Deliver
items.detail: Send the appropriate link or summary to named recipients.

items.label: Act / alert
items.detail: Route a genuine exception to the responsible owner.

sections.takeaway: An automatically emailed stale report is still a stale report.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: The audience determines the detail
sections.explanation: A client, a channel operator and a leadership team need different levels of detail from the same evidence.

items.label: Owner / client
items.detail: Outcome, cost, one recommendation and one ask.

items.label: Operator
items.detail: Channel diagnostics, tests, data checks and next tasks.

items.label: Leadership
items.detail: Progress against goal, risks and required decisions.

sections.takeaway: Keep definitions consistent even when you simplify the presentation.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: Which of the five panels stops a dashboard becoming decorative?
checkpoint.answer: The insight notes connect the evidence to a decision, owner and date. They rely on the other panels for a trustworthy diagnosis.

sections.section: 5. Reporting cadence and the audience principle

m6-t4.introduction: Separate credit assignment from causal impact. Use experiments and explicit decision rules to learn before reallocating a budget.

sections.title: One journey, several credit stories
sections.explanation: The same observed sale can be attributed differently without changing the underlying customer journey.

items.label: First-touch view
items.detail: Emphasises the observed discovery touch.

items.label: Last-touch view
items.detail: Emphasises the observed final interaction.

items.label: Multi-touch / data-driven
items.detail: Distributes credit using rules or platform modelling.

sections.takeaway: Attribution is a reporting model, not proof of incrementality. Compare only compatible models and windows.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: The counterfactual is the hard question
sections.explanation: Incrementality asks what would have happened without the marketing activity.

items.label: Observed activity
items.detail: Customers bought during the campaign.

items.label: Counterfactual
items.detail: Some might have bought even if the campaign had not run.

items.label: Designed comparison
items.detail: Use an appropriate holdout or carefully planned test where feasible.

sections.takeaway: A simple before/after pause test is vulnerable to seasonality and other changes; state those limitations.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 2. The honest question: "would it have happened anyway?"

sections.title: A difference is not automatically a winner
sections.explanation: In this synthetic equal-sized comparison, A has 50 signups from 1,000 eligible visitors and B has 60 from 1,000.

items.label: A: current page
items.detail: 50 ÷ 1,000. Same event definition and observation window.

items.label: B: changed headline
items.detail: 60 ÷ 1,000. One intended variable changed.

sections.takeaway: The observed lift is 1 percentage point, or 20% relative. That alone does not establish significance or practical value; use the planned sample and decision rule.
sections.caption: Synthetic worked example, not live campaign data or an industry benchmark.
sections.section: 3. A/B testing: the experiment that settles arguments

sections.title: Turn a finding into the next controlled step
sections.explanation: Learning compounds when the experiment’s result becomes an explicit operational decision.

items.label: Hypothesise
items.detail: Name one change, its mechanism and expected useful outcome.

items.label: Design
items.detail: Set assignment, sample, duration and guardrails in advance.

items.label: Evaluate
items.detail: Check data quality and the planned decision rule.

items.label: Decide
items.detail: Ship, revise or stop, and record what was learned.

sections.takeaway: Do not repeatedly peek and stop as soon as a preferred result appears.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: Does a data-driven attribution report prove a channel caused its credited sales?
checkpoint.answer: No. It assigns credit within the available data and model. Causal impact needs an appropriate experimental design or a clearly qualified incrementality analysis.

sections.section: 4. The optimisation loop: from findings to actions

m6-pb4.introduction: Build the dashboard around a decision and an insight log. Keep sources, simulated data and experimental assumptions visible throughout the pack.

sections.title: A dashboard is the middle, not the end
sections.explanation: The project begins with a business question and ends with a justified action.

items.label: Question
items.detail: Name the decision and the KPI tree.

items.label: Evidence
items.detail: Verify sources, definitions and event quality.

items.label: View
items.detail: Build five panels that answer clear questions.

items.label: Decision
items.detail: Write the diagnosis, action, owner and review date.

sections.takeaway: A chart without an insight log does not fulfil the project’s central purpose.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: The submission joins data and judgement
sections.explanation: Keep the dashboard, experiment designs and client communication connected to the same evidence.

items.label: Measurement design
items.detail: KPI tree, source names, event plan and verification step.

items.label: Dashboard
items.detail: Five panels with comparisons and a visible manual layer.

items.label: Insight log
items.detail: Four dated entries with diagnosis, actions and owners.

items.label: Experiments
items.detail: Incrementality design and an A/B plan with a pre-written rule.

items.label: Delivery + integrity
items.detail: Automation choices, client email and specific AI disclosure.

sections.takeaway: Label demo-property and simulated data at the point where it is shown, not only in a footnote.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Four learning strands must meet
sections.explanation: A visually attractive report is incomplete if it omits measurement definitions or the reasoning behind a decision.

items.label: 6.1: decision metric
items.detail: Explain which decision each headline number informs.

items.label: 6.2: events
items.detail: Choose and verify a meaningful key event.

items.label: 6.3: reporting
items.detail: Use the five-panel structure and an appropriate delivery process.

items.label: 6.4: honest inference
items.detail: Show attribution limits or an appropriate experiment design.

sections.takeaway: Do not treat the platform’s attributed conversions as a causal estimate of campaign impact.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Build in an order that protects data quality
sections.explanation: A small reconciliation check early in the project prevents a large misleading dashboard later.

items.label: Tree + sources
items.detail: Define measures and verify the available data.

items.label: Connect + check
items.detail: Reconcile dates, spend, events and duplicates.

items.label: Build + interpret
items.detail: Create the panels and four insight entries.

items.label: Design + communicate
items.detail: Finish experiments and the client-ready recommendation.

sections.takeaway: Check the assessor can open the final dashboard or evidence screenshots.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Make the professional standard observable
sections.explanation: The rubric values the quality of the decision process as much as the chart layout.

items.label: Reliable measurement
items.detail: Definitions, sources, comparisons and guardrails are explicit.

items.label: Reasoned action
items.detail: Insight and experiment plans have owners and pre-written rules.

items.label: Honest communication
items.detail: The client understands the recommendation and all simulation is labelled.

sections.takeaway: Use the original rubric and its stated pass rule. This visual groups the ideas but does not alter criteria or marks.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: Can a simulated insight log be submitted as if it came from a live campaign?
checkpoint.answer: No. Label simulation and the data source clearly in every relevant view. Keep the distinction between an observed result, a forecast and a proposed experiment visible.
